original_question: For perturbations of the focusing nonlinear Schrodinger equation of the form i u_tilde_t + u_tilde_xx + 2 |u_tilde|^2 u_tilde + epsilon |u_tilde|^ell u_tilde = 0 with decaying initial data, can one analyze the long-time behavior of solutions, especially in the case where the initial data correspond to a two-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing NLS equation?
target_in_paper: Problem 7 (additional problems for integrable systems): the open problem of analyzing the Cauchy problem for perturbations of the focusing NLS equation (13), especially when the initial datum corresponds to a 2-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing NLS.
correct_elements: Your draft already identifies the correct open problem, the correct focusing perturbed NLS equation (13), the decaying-data Cauchy setting, the emphasis on long-time analysis, and the paper's explicit special interest in initial data coming from a 2-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing NLS.
missing_details: The paper states this as a Cauchy problem on the full line x in R, with initial condition u_tilde(x,0)=f_tilde(x) and f_tilde(x)->0 as |x|->infinity.

The nearby context treats the exponent ell in the perturbative regime relevant to the comparison with the defocusing result: the quoted defocusing theorem required ell>7/2 for technical reasons, and the author says ell>2 should be enough there; the smallness heuristic for the perturbation term is explicitly tied to ell>2.

The official formulation asks to 'analyze solutions of the Cauchy problem,' not only vaguely to study perturbations; the long-time t->infinity behavior is the main nearby benchmark because the preceding defocusing result is described asymptotically.
The draft omits the key obstruction emphasized in the paper: unlike the defocusing case, one cannot expect a general sup-norm decay estimate because solitons are present.
The paper's singled-out special case is that f_tilde corresponds to a 2-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing NLS, i.e. the epsilon=0 equation.
The problem is narrowly about this specific power-type perturbation of the focusing cubic NLS; the paper does not broaden it here to arbitrary perturbations or general nonlinearities.

To make the question fully stand-alone, it helps to specify the ambient analytic setting explicitly: u_tilde is the NLS field on the line, implicitly complex-valued, with x the spatial variable and t the time variable.

The surrounding discussion uses epsilon as a perturbation parameter; the immediately preceding defocusing result is for suitably small positive epsilon, so the perturbative reading should be kept in view even though the open problem for the focusing equation is stated informally.
refined_question: For a fixed exponent ell in the regime highlighted by the adjacent discussion (in particular ell>2), consider the Cauchy problem on the real line for the focusing perturbed nonlinear Schrödinger equation i (u_tilde)_t + (u_tilde)_{xx} + 2|u_tilde|^2 u_tilde + epsilon |u_tilde|^ell u_tilde = 0, with initial data u_tilde(x,0)=f_tilde(x) satisfying f_tilde(x)->0 as |x|->infinity. Can one analyze solutions of this Cauchy problem, especially their behavior as t->infinity, in the particularly important case where f_tilde is the initial profile of a 2-soliton solution of the unperturbed focusing NLS (epsilon=0), despite the fact that the sup-norm decay mechanism available in the defocusing problem breaks down because of solitons?
justification: The draft matches almost verbatim the first open problem inside Problem 7. On page 17, immediately after recalling the defocusing perturbed NLS problem (12) and its asymptotic behavior, Deift asks for an analysis of the focusing perturbed NLS Cauchy problem (13), explicitly says that the case where f_tilde corresponds to a 2-soliton of the unperturbed focusing NLS is 'of particular interest,' and explains that the main new difficulty is the loss of the sup-norm decay used in the defocusing argument because solitons can persist. I therefore kept the question tightly focused on equation (13) and only made explicit the line/Cauchy-data setting and the exponent/perturbative context supplied by the adjacent discussion.
